title: pg_scann SOAR spill — centroid-probe lever (SIFT1M, in-Postgres A/B vs no-SOAR)
dataset: SIFT1M — full 1,000,000 base, 200 queries, official ground-truth (valid at 1M)
hardware: DigitalOcean droplet 8 vCPU / 16 GB (ams3), single-threaded, pg17, warm cache
method: Two tables IDENTICAL data (M46 A/B): siftsoar → v5 (separate_storage=1) WITH soar_lambda=1000 (λ=1.0); siftbase → v5 (separate_storage=1) no SOAR; lists=500, pq_subspaces=32. Swept over_fetch ∈ {8,16} × probes ∈ {4..64}. recall@10 vs official GT; QPS best-of-3.
design: SOAR (Sun et al. NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2404.00774): each vector spilled to a SECOND list chosen by the orthogonality-amplified residual loss L(c')=‖v-c'‖²+λ·⟨v-c',r⟩²/‖r‖² (r=v-c1). ivf.rs with_soar_spill (~40 LoC, exact argmin over all centroids); soar_lambda reloption. Scan dedup-by-tid via the existing amgettuple emitted-HashSet (no scan change).
correctness: 247 pg_tests GREEN (246 + 1 SOAR: ambuild_ivf_soar_spill_scans_high_recall_no_dupes — verifies no duplicate ids in top-k despite each vector in 2 lists), 0 failed — zero regression.

index_size_mb.note: SOAR DOUBLED the index (not the paper's +7.7-17.3%) — in the v5 per-list VECTOR region the spilled vector's FULL f32 is packed in both lists (list_entries returns it fully in both). The paper duplicates only the CODE (f32 single-copy via a global vector store); this minimal impl duplicates f32 too. Fixing it needs a global-vector-store layout (deferred — see verdict).

build_s.note: SOAR +~3min for the extra secondary-assignment pass (argmin over all centroids)

findings: The centroid-probe lever IS REAL: at LOW probes SOAR reaches materially higher recall than no-SOAR — probes=4: +0.12 (0.89 vs 0.77), probes=8: +0.06-0.07. Fewer probes reach a given recall, exactly the SOAR promise (Fig. 10).

BUT it does NOT yield a QPS win on SIFT1M warm-cache: SOAR is slower at EVERY point (qps_ratio 0.66-0.80). Two causes: (a) the index doubled (f32 duplicated in this minimal impl), so each probe reads ~2× the candidates; (b) SIFT1M's high-recall bind is the Stage-2 f32 random-read (M84/M85), NOT the probe count — SOAR attacks the wrong axis for this dataset/regime.
SOAR's recall ceiling is capped ~0.98 (vs base's 0.99+) because spilled duplicates occupy rerank-pool slots (deduped at emit, but the pool is finite) — at high probes the gain goes negative.
This is the exact HONEST-NEGATIVE the M86 deep research predicted: 'SOAR helps the probe axis; M84 measured our SIFT1M bind is the Stage-2 read, not probes — be willing to return honest-negative.'
honest_caveats: The 2× index is an IMPLEMENTATION artifact, not inherent to SOAR: the paper's +7.7-17.3% assumes only the CODE is duplicated (f32 stored once globally). The v5 per-list VECTOR region duplicates the f32 too. A global-vector-store redesign would fix the storage — but since SOAR gives no SIFT1M QPS win even at +15% (the probe axis isn't the bind), that redesign is DEFERRED (YAGNI) until a regime where probe-reduction pays off (billion-scale / very-high-nlist, M88).
SOAR's benefit grows with N and recall (paper Fig. 10) — it may pay off at billion-scale where many probes are needed and memory bandwidth (not the small-N Stage-2 read) dominates. Not measured here.
The feature ships opt-in (WITH soar_lambda=N, default 0=off). Correct + tested; its measured SIFT1M value is a low-probe recall lever, not a QPS win.
north_star_context: M86 honestly measures SOAR as NOT the SIFT1M QPS lever (the probe axis is not our bind — the Stage-2 read is, which M85 SQ8 addresses). The centroid-probe lever is real and may pay off at billion-scale (M88). Correct, opt-in, honest-negative — measurement-first (like M82). Still class-AlloyDB-in-Postgres; NOT a ScaNN-library beat (M73/ADR-0035).
